scoreNote: Strong (5): grants the reason's insight about perspective, then shows it cannot support the claim — decisions cannot wait for hindsight, the past we use is already distant, and even rough connections instruct; engages the specific reason.

sentences.text: Historians often say we cannot judge our own era clearly until it has cooled into history.

From this the claim concludes that knowing about the past cannot help people make important decisions today, reasoning that we cannot connect current events to past ones until we have gained some distance from both.

The reason contains a real insight about perspective, but it does not support the claim: we already possess ample distance from the past, present decisions cannot wait for hindsight, and even tentative connections to history are better than none.
The claim asks the impossible of decision-makers: to wait for a clarity that only the future can supply.
Important decisions cannot be postponed until events have aged into tidy lessons, for leaders, doctors, and individuals must act now, with whatever understanding they can muster.
If we could use the past only after attaining perfect distance, we could never use it at all, since by then new decisions would already be pressing upon us.
A guide that may be consulted only in hindsight is no guide for the choices we face today.

sections.role: Body — We already have distance from the past

sentences.text: However, the reason misstates our actual situation.
We need distance only from the present, and we are not connecting two equally close events, because the past in question is already remote, studied, and understood.
When we draw on the fall of an empire, a financial panic of a century ago, or a long-settled war, we are using events from which ample time has already passed.
The decision-maker stands at a vantage the reason ignores, looking back on a distant, well-documented past to help interpret a present she is still living through.
We are rarely asked to connect two unformed moments; usually we read a settled past to illuminate an unsettled present.
Moreover, even connections made without full hindsight are valuable.
We need not perfectly match a present event to a past one for history to be useful, since a rough analogy can still warn, suggest, and prepare.
Recognizing that a current crisis rhymes with an earlier one, even imperfectly, can prompt us to ask better questions and avoid mistakes already on record.
Even a partial parallel can flag a danger that would otherwise pass unnoticed, turning a vague sense of unease into a specific, answerable question and buying us time to prepare.
The reason at most counsels humility about our judgments, urging us to hold them provisionally; it does not show that the past cannot help, only that it must be used with care.
Imperfect lessons, applied modestly, still beat facing the present with no memory at all.
In conclusion, the reason rightly reminds us that perspective improves with time, but the claim it is meant to support does not follow.

Because decisions cannot wait for hindsight, because the past we consult is already at a distance, and because even tentative connections instruct us, knowing about the past remains a genuine help to present choices.
We cannot wait for history to ripen before we act; we must let the history we already have guide us now.
